title: Change Orders and Hidden Conditions in a Rehab
metaDescription: What is commonly hidden behind walls, under floors and in sewer laterals, how to size a rehab contingency, and what a fair change-order process looks like.
h1: Change Orders and Unforeseen Conditions: How Investors Plan for What the Walls Are Hiding
dek: Every rehab has conditions nobody can see at the walkthrough: rot under flooring, failed drains, outdated wiring inside walls, a broken sewer lateral. You cannot eliminate surprises, but you can predict where they cluster, size a contingency to match the house, and insist on a change-order process that is written, priced and approved before work proceeds.
keyTakeaways: Hidden conditions cluster in predictable places: wet areas, behind old plaster, under layered flooring, in foundations and in the sewer lateral.
Contingency should be sized to the risk of the specific house, its age, vacancy history, prior repairs and how much of it you plan to open up.
Pre-purchase investigation such as a sewer scope, a moisture check and targeted inspections turns some unknowns into line items.
A good change order is written, describes the condition with photos, prices the fix, states the schedule effect and is approved before work proceeds.
Most change-order disputes start with a vague original scope, so the best protection is a detailed scope with clear allowances and exclusions.

sections.h2: Why are hidden conditions unavoidable in a rehab?
sections.body:
A walkthrough shows you surfaces. Paint, flooring, cabinets, siding and ceilings are exactly the things that hide the condition of a house's structure and systems. Many distressed and older houses have also been patched, flipped or covered up more than once, so what you see may be the second or third layer of finish over a problem.

Some things cannot be confirmed without destructive investigation. You can't see the condition of a subfloor under three layers of vinyl, the framing behind a tiled shower, the wiring inside a plaster wall, or the joint between a cast-iron stack and a newer PVC repair without opening something up. A seller is unlikely to let you remove a bathroom floor before closing.

The goal is not to predict every surprise. It is to recognize the categories where surprises are common, investigate what you reasonably can before purchase, price a contingency that reflects the remaining uncertainty, and agree with your contractor on how changes will be handled before demolition starts.

Investors who do this well tend to have fewer large surprises, not because their houses are better but because they treated the likely ones as scope items from the beginning. The contingency then covers the genuinely unforeseeable, rather than the predictable condition that nobody priced.

sections.h2: What is commonly hidden behind walls and ceilings?
sections.body:
Walls and ceilings hide the systems that an inspector can only partly assess from outlets, fixtures and the panel.

Electrical. In older houses, original knob-and-tube wiring may still be live inside walls even when visible circuits have been updated. Ungrounded two-wire circuits, cloth-insulated cable, aluminum branch wiring in some houses from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s, overloaded or spliced connections without junction boxes, and amateur additions are all common finds. Once walls are opened, an electrician may recommend or a code official may require more updating than the original scope assumed.

Plumbing. Galvanized steel supply lines corrode from the inside and can look fine at the fittings while being badly restricted. Drain lines may be cast iron with cracked or scaled sections, or a mix of materials joined poorly. Polybutylene supply piping, used in some houses from the late 1970s into the mid-1990s, is another find that changes scope.

Water damage and mold. Slow leaks behind showers, under windows and around roof penetrations rot framing and sheathing long before stains appear on the surface. Fresh paint over a ceiling stain is a common sign that something was covered rather than fixed.

Structure. Previously removed or cut framing, notched joists, missing headers over altered openings and undersized beams appear when walls and ceilings are opened, especially in houses with past remodels.

Hazardous materials. Asbestos may be present in older plaster, joint compound, pipe insulation, duct wrap and textured ceilings. Lead paint is likely in pre-1978 houses. Both affect how demolition can proceed.

sections.h2: What is commonly hidden under floors and below grade?
sections.body:
Floors and foundations are where some of the most expensive surprises live.

Subfloors in kitchens, bathrooms and laundry areas are frequently damaged by long-term leaks from toilets, tubs, dishwashers and washing machines. Layers of vinyl or tile installed over each other can hide soft, delaminated or rotted plywood and plank subfloor, and sometimes damaged joists underneath.

Old flooring itself can be a factor. Some older resilient tile and its adhesive contain asbestos, and removing it requires care or professional abatement depending on local rules and condition.

Framing under floors can show sagging from undersized joists, notches cut for plumbing, failed sister repairs, or damage from insects and moisture in crawlspaces.

Foundations can hide cracking, settlement, bowing walls, deteriorated mortar in older masonry, and water intrusion that shows up only after finishes are removed or the season changes. Finished basements are particularly good at hiding foundation issues behind paneling and carpet.

The sewer lateral, the pipe running from the house to the municipal sewer or septic system, is one of the most common and most overlooked hidden conditions. Older clay, cast-iron and Orangeburg laterals can be cracked, offset, sagging or invaded by tree roots. Many houses show no symptoms while vacant because little water is going down the drains. The problem appears when a full household moves in.

In many places the owner is responsible for the lateral from the house to the main, and in some cities the connection at the main as well. Replacement can involve excavation in a yard, driveway or right-of-way, which brings permits and restoration costs.

sections.h2: How can you reduce unknowns before you buy?
sections.body:
You cannot open every wall, but targeted, mostly non-destructive investigation converts some unknowns into known line items.

Useful pre-purchase checks include:
- A sewer scope, a camera inspection of the lateral, especially on older houses, houses with large trees near the line, and vacant houses where low water use may mask a problem
- A moisture meter or thermal camera scan around showers, tubs, toilets, windows and below roof valleys
- A close look at the electrical panel, service size and any visible wiring in the basement, attic or crawlspace
- Identification of supply and drain pipe materials where they are exposed
- An inspection of the attic for roof leaks, ventilation issues and evidence of past fire or pest activity
- A look at the foundation from the inside and outside, noting cracks, efflorescence, water lines and repairs
- Permit history, to see what was done legally and what may have been done without permits
- Testing for asbestos or lead in materials you plan to disturb, where the purchase timeline allows

Bank-owned and vacant houses often have additional unknowns because they may have been winterized, de-winterized or left unheated, and plumbing that looks intact may fail a pressure test. If the utilities are off, ask whether a pressure test or a limited de-winterization is possible during due diligence.

A free Pre-Offer Rehab Review from Genstone is one way to bring an estimator's eye to these questions before you commit capital. Whoever does it, the aim is the same: price the risk you can see and narrow the risk you cannot.

sections.h2: How should you size a contingency?
sections.body:
Contingency is the money set aside for conditions you could not reasonably know at the time of scope. It is not a slush fund for upgrades, and it is not a substitute for a complete scope.

Rather than using one fixed rule for every house, size contingency to the risk factors of the specific property. Factors that call for a larger contingency include:
- Age, particularly older houses with original systems or multiple generations of repairs
- Extended vacancy, freeze exposure or evidence of past water events
- Visible signs of patched or covered-over damage, such as fresh paint on ceilings or new flooring in a house that is otherwise neglected
- Scope that opens a lot of the house, such as a gut, layout change or full systems replacement
- Limited access during due diligence
- Older or unknown sewer laterals with no scope
- Prior unpermitted work that may need correction

Factors that support a smaller contingency include a newer house, a cosmetic scope that does not open walls or floors, recent permitted systems work you can verify, and thorough pre-purchase investigation.

Keep contingency as a separate, visible line in your budget rather than padding individual line items. That way you can see how much of it you have used and make a deliberate decision when a change comes in. If you finish under budget, the contingency is profit. If you pad everything, you lose that visibility.

Also plan for schedule contingency. A hidden condition costs money to fix and adds days to the project, and holding costs continue while it is being resolved.

sections.h2: What does a good change-order process look like?
sections.body:
A change order is a written modification to the contract scope, price or schedule. A good process protects both sides and keeps the job moving.

The elements to insist on:
- Discovery and documentation. When a crew finds a condition outside the scope, the contractor documents it with photos and a plain explanation of what was found, where, and why it matters.
- Options where they exist. Some conditions have one fix. Others have alternatives, such as repair versus replace, or a minimum code fix versus a fuller upgrade. A good contractor lays them out.
- Written pricing. The change order states the cost of the added work, and any credit for work no longer needed, using the same pricing basis as the original contract.
- Schedule effect. The change order says whether and how the work affects the completion date.
- Approval before proceeding. Except for genuine emergencies, such as an active leak or a structural safety issue, work outside scope should not proceed until the owner approves in writing.
- Integration with draws. Approved change orders are added to the draw schedule so payment is tied to completion like the rest of the work.

Agree on this process before work starts. The contract should state how change orders are requested, priced and approved, who can approve them on your side, and how quickly you will respond. A slow approval process is itself a schedule risk, since crews may have to stop or move to other tasks while waiting.

On remote projects, photo and video documentation is what makes fast decisions possible. Genstone's projects keep progress and milestones visible without the client being on site, which is the kind of visibility that lets change orders be approved quickly and on evidence.

sections.h2: How do you avoid change-order disputes?
sections.body:
Most disputes over change orders are really disputes over the original scope. If the contract said renovate bathroom, every disagreement about what that included becomes a fight about whether something is a change.

The fix is a detailed scope. A good scope document lists each room or system, what is being done, the materials or finish level, quantities where they matter, and what is excluded. It also identifies allowances, budgeted amounts for items not yet selected, such as tile or light fixtures, and states what happens if selections come in above or below the allowance.

Explicit exclusions matter as much as inclusions. If the scope excludes sewer lateral work, asbestos abatement, or work behind walls beyond a certain extent, everyone knows that discovering those conditions will produce a change order. That is not a gotcha; it is honesty about what was priced.

Other practices that prevent disputes:
- Separate owner-requested upgrades from unforeseen-condition changes in your records, so you can see why the budget moved
- Avoid verbal approvals on site; confirm in writing even if it is a text or email
- Ask for unit pricing for common variable items, like per-sheet subfloor replacement or per-foot drain line replacement, so changes can be priced quickly against an agreed rate
- Review change orders promptly so they do not pile up into a large, contentious bill at the end

When the scope is specific, real changes are easy to identify and price. When it is vague, every change is an argument.

sections.h2: Which changes should you approve, and which should you push back on?
sections.body:
Not every change order is a must-do. Evaluate each against your exit strategy.

Generally approve changes that address safety, code compliance, water intrusion, structure, or a condition that will be flagged by a buyer's inspector or appraiser. Leaving a rotted subfloor under new tile, closing walls over active knob-and-tube wiring, or ignoring a broken sewer lateral turns a known problem into a future one, usually at a worse time and a higher cost.

Look harder at changes that are upgrades rather than fixes. Sometimes a contractor proposes a fuller replacement where a repair would meet code and satisfy the exit buyer. Ask whether the minimum compliant fix is available and what the trade-offs are. On a flip, the question is whether the upgrade shows up in value or in a smoother sale. On a rental hold, it is whether it reduces maintenance and turn costs over the hold.

Push back on changes that should have been in the original scope. If a condition was visible at the walkthrough, such as a sagging floor or a panel with an obvious defect, and the contractor did not price it, that is a scope gap. How you handle it depends on your contract, but it is a different conversation than a genuinely hidden condition.

Finally, watch the cumulative effect. Each individual change may be reasonable while the total consumes your contingency and margin. Review the running total against the budget at every draw, and revisit your exit numbers if the total climbs.

faqs.q: What is a reasonable contingency for a rehab?
faqs.a: There is no single correct figure. Contingency should match the risk profile of the specific house: older age, long vacancy, past water events, visible covered-up damage, unknown sewer condition and a scope that opens many walls and floors all justify more. A newer house with a cosmetic scope and verified systems needs less. Keep contingency as its own budget line rather than padding each item, so you can see when you are drawing on it and decide deliberately.

faqs.q: Is a sewer scope worth it before buying a rental or flip?
faqs.a: On older houses, houses with mature trees near the line, and houses that have been vacant, a sewer scope is one of the most useful inexpensive inspections available. Lateral problems often stay hidden while a house is empty because little water is flowing. The camera shows the pipe material and any cracks, offsets, sags or roots. Knowing the lateral's condition before closing lets you price repair or negotiate rather than discover it after tenants or buyers move in.

faqs.q: Should a contractor proceed with extra work without my approval?
faqs.a: Generally no. The exception is a true emergency, such as an active leak, a structural hazard or an unsafe electrical condition, where stopping the immediate danger is reasonable and documentation follows. For everything else, the contractor should document the condition, price the change in writing and wait for approval. Agree on this in the contract, including who on your side can approve changes and how quickly you will respond, so work does not stall.

faqs.q: How do change orders affect lender draws?
faqs.a: If your rehab is financed with a construction or fix-and-flip loan that holds back rehab funds, approved change orders may need lender approval to be paid from the rehab budget, and some lenders require a budget revision. Changes that exceed the held-back funds come from your own cash. Tell your lender early when significant hidden conditions appear, and keep change orders documented with photos so inspections and draw requests line up with the revised scope.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an allowance and a change order?
faqs.a: An allowance is a budgeted amount in the original contract for an item not yet selected, such as tile, lighting or appliances. If your selection costs more or less than the allowance, the difference is adjusted, usually through a simple reconciliation. A change order modifies the scope itself, adding, removing or altering work. Allowances keep the original scope moving before selections are final; change orders handle new conditions or new decisions after the contract is signed.
